questions.stem: The monetary principle means that:
options: only items that can be measured in money are recorded, in one currency
every asset is recorded at its current market value each year
the owner's personal transactions are kept out of the business records
the business is assumed to continue operating into the future
questions.explanation: The monetary principle requires transactions to be measured in a common unit, Australian dollars for an Australian business, so items like staff morale are not recorded. Keeping private transactions out is the entity concept, and continuing operation is going concern.

questions.stem: Bottlebrush Bakery bought land for $300,000. Five years later the land is valued at $450,000. Under the historical cost principle, at what amount is the land recorded?
questions.explanation: Historical cost records assets at their original cost, which is verifiable from the purchase documents. The $450,000 valuation is an estimate and is not recorded, and $150,000 is only the increase.

questions.stem: Bottlebrush Bakery buys a $15 stapler expected to last five years and records it as an expense rather than as a non-current asset. Which principle justifies this?
options: materiality, because the amount is too small to affect users' decisions
historical cost, because the stapler must be recorded at its original price
going concern, because the bakery will still operate in five years
monetary, because the stapler cannot be measured in Australian dollars
questions.explanation: Materiality allows small items to be treated in the simplest way when doing so would not change any user's decisions. The stapler can be measured in money, and going concern would, if anything, suggest spreading its cost.

questions.stem: The owner of a business announces it will close and sell all its assets next month. Which principle can no longer be applied in preparing its reports?
options: double entry
going concern
accounting entity
monetary
questions.explanation: Going concern assumes the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future, which justifies valuing assets at cost less depreciation. Once closure is certain, assets should reflect what they will sell for.

questions.stem: Bottlebrush Bakery has assets of $86,000 and liabilities of $31,000. What is its net worth?
questions.explanation: Net worth = assets − liabilities = 86,000 − 31,000 = $55,000, which equals owner's equity. Adding the two figures gives $117,000, which has no meaning.

questions.stem: The principle of double entry means that every transaction:
options: involves both a cash payment and a cash receipt
affects at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits
is recorded twice in the same account to make sure that it is never missed
is recorded once by the owner and again by an outside accountant
questions.explanation: Each transaction has at least two effects, recorded as equal debits and credits, which keeps the accounting equation in balance. Recording twice in one account would double-count it.

questions.stem: Under double entry, which change is recorded as a credit?
options: an increase in drawings
an increase in a liability
an increase in an asset
an increase in an expense
questions.explanation: Liabilities, owner's equity and revenue increase on the credit side. Assets, expenses and drawings increase on the debit side.

questions.stem: Mia opens a business with Bank $6,000, Equipment $14,000, Inventories $9,000 and a Loan of $12,000. In the opening entry, what amount is credited to Capital?
questions.explanation: Capital = assets − liabilities = (6,000 + 14,000 + 9,000) − 12,000 = $17,000. The assets are debited, and the loan and capital are credited so that debits equal credits.

questions.stem: A business sells an old printer for cash at its book value of $400. Ignoring GST and depreciation, which entry is recorded?
options: Dr Bank 400; Cr Capital 400
Dr Bank 400; Cr Office Equipment 400
Dr Office Equipment 400; Cr Bank 400
Dr Bank 400; Cr Sales 400
questions.explanation: Selling an asset at book value swaps one asset (equipment) for another (cash), with no gain or loss. It is not Sales, because the printer was not inventory, and it is not a capital contribution.

questions.stem: A business sells inventory that cost $600 for $900 cash, using the perpetual inventory system. Ignoring GST, which entries are recorded?
options: Dr Cost of Goods Sold 900, Cr Sales 900; and Dr Bank 600, Cr Inventories 600
Dr Bank 900, Cr Sales 900; and Dr Cost of Goods Sold 600, Cr Inventories 600
Dr Bank 900, Cr Inventories 900; with no entry for the cost of the goods
Dr Bank 300, Cr Sales 300; recording only the profit on the sale
questions.explanation: Under the perpetual system each sale records the revenue at selling price and transfers the cost of the goods from Inventories to Cost of Goods Sold, so inventory records are always up to date. Recording only the profit would understate both sales and cost.

questions.stem: A business pays $2,750 including GST for repairs. How much GST is included?
questions.explanation: GST is 10% of the GST-exclusive price, so the GST in an inclusive amount is one eleventh: 2,750 ÷ 11 = $250. Taking 10% of the inclusive amount gives $275, which is wrong.

questions.stem: A business provides a service on credit for $1,650 including GST. How is the amount split in its records?
options: $1,500 revenue and $150 GST owed to the business by the ATO
$1,500 revenue and $150 GST owed to the Australian Taxation Office
$1,650 revenue and $165 GST owed to the Australian Taxation Office
$1,485 revenue and $165 GST owed to the Australian Taxation Office
questions.explanation: The GST-exclusive amount, 1,650 ÷ 1.1 = $1,500, is revenue, and the $150 GST collected is a liability to the ATO. The customer owes the full $1,650.

questions.stem: Which supply is GST-free?
options: a new car sold by a dealer
fresh fruit sold at a greengrocer
a meal served at a restaurant
rent on a residential house
questions.explanation: Basic food such as fresh fruit is GST-free. Restaurant meals and new cars are taxable supplies, and residential rent is input taxed.

questions.stem: A supply is input taxed, such as residential rent. This means the supplier:
options: charges GST at double the normal rate and claims no credits on any of its purchases
charges no GST on the supply and cannot claim GST credits on related purchases
charges no GST on the supply but can claim GST credits on related purchases
charges GST on the supply and can claim GST credits on related purchases
questions.explanation: Input taxed supplies have no GST charged, but the supplier also cannot claim credits for GST paid on inputs. A GST-free supply has no GST charged and the supplier can still claim credits.

questions.stem: An Australian Business Number (ABN) is:
options: the number printed on every product a business sells to customers
a bank account number used only for paying GST to the government
a licence number issued to accountants by their professional body after they qualify
a unique number that identifies a business in its dealings with the ATO and others
questions.explanation: An ABN identifies a business to government and other businesses and is needed to register for GST. It appears on tax invoices so customers can claim GST credits.

questions.stem: A Business Activity Statement (BAS) is used to:
options: list each customer's balance and how long it has been owing
record the receipt of cash from credit customers each day
report and pay GST and other tax amounts to the Australian Taxation Office
show the owner's assets, liabilities and equity at the end of the year
questions.explanation: A business lodges a BAS with the ATO to report GST collected and GST credits, and to pay the net amount or claim a refund, along with other taxes such as PAYG withholding. The Statement of Financial Position shows assets, liabilities and equity.

questions.stem: For the quarter, a business collected GST of $4,800 on its sales and paid GST of $3,100 on its purchases. What does its BAS show?
options: $4,800 payable to the ATO
$1,700 payable to the ATO
$1,700 refundable by the ATO
$7,900 payable to the ATO
questions.explanation: The net GST = 4,800 − 3,100 = $1,700. GST collected exceeds GST credits, so the business pays the difference. A refund arises only when credits exceed GST collected.

questions.stem: Why is GST collected on sales excluded from revenue?
options: it is an expense of the business that is recorded when sales are made
it belongs to the customer and must be refunded at the end of the year
it is collected on behalf of the ATO, so it is a liability, not income of the business
it is too small an amount to be material, so it is ignored in all of the business's records
questions.explanation: The business acts as a collector for the government, so GST on sales is owed to the ATO and recorded as a liability. Including it in revenue would overstate profit.

questions.stem: An adjustment note is issued when:
options: a business lodges its Business Activity Statement with the ATO at the end of the quarter
a price is reduced or goods are returned after a tax invoice, adjusting the GST
a customer pays the full amount of an invoice by the due date
the owner takes cash from the business for personal use
questions.explanation: An adjustment note records a change to an earlier taxable sale, such as a return or a price reduction, and adjusts the GST. A customer's payment is evidenced by a receipt or remittance advice.

questions.stem: Bottlebrush Bakery buys flour from a supplier on 30-day terms. This is:
options: a cash transaction, because GST is included in the price
a credit transaction, creating an account payable
a cash transaction, because the flour is received immediately
a credit transaction, creating an account receivable
questions.explanation: When payment is made later, the purchase is a credit transaction and the business owes the supplier, an account payable. Accounts receivable are amounts customers owe the business.

questions.stem: Which is an acceptable source document for a payment made by electronic funds transfer?
options: the EFT confirmation or remittance advice, matched to the bank statement
a verbal agreement with the supplier made over the telephone
the owner's memory of the amount paid, written into the journal a few weeks later
a photograph of the goods that were purchased
questions.explanation: Electronic documents such as EFT confirmations, emailed invoices and bank statements provide verifiable evidence of transactions. Verbal agreements and memory cannot be checked.

questions.stem: Compared with a T format ledger account, a columnar (running balance) ledger account:
options: shows the account balance after every entry
shows only the closing balance at the end of the year
records debits and credits in the same column
does not need cross-references to other accounts
questions.explanation: Columnar ledgers have debit, credit and balance columns, so the balance is updated after each entry. T accounts are balanced only when required.

questions.stem: A chart of accounts is:
options: the final statement prepared at the end of the reporting period
a list of all the business's ledger accounts, grouped by element and numbered
a graph of the business's revenue and expenses over the past year
a list of the business's customers and the amounts they owe
questions.explanation: The chart of accounts lists every account, usually numbered by type (assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses), so transactions are classified consistently and reports can be generated. A list of customers is the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger.

questions.stem: A trial balance does not agree. What is a sensible first step to locate the error?
options: delete the ledger and re-enter the year's transactions
re-add the debit and credit columns of the trial balance
record a correcting entry for the difference to Capital
prepare the Statement of Profit or Loss and see if it balances
questions.explanation: Errors are found by working backwards from the simplest checks: re-add the columns, then check that balances were transferred correctly, then check each ledger balance and posting. Forcing the difference into Capital hides the error.

questions.stem: The debit column of a trial balance exceeds the credit column by $1,000. Which error could explain this?
options: a $500 receipt was recorded as $50 in both the Bank and Accounts Receivable accounts
a $500 credit to Sales was posted to the debit side of the Sales account
a $1,000 credit sale was not recorded in the journal at all
a $1,000 payment was debited to Rent instead of to Wages
questions.explanation: Posting a $500 credit as a debit adds $500 to the debit column and removes $500 from the credit column, a difference of $1,000. Omissions, entries to the wrong account and the same wrong amount on both sides do not upset the trial balance.

questions.stem: A control account is:
options: an account used only by the owner to record private transactions
a bank account that requires two signatures for every payment
the account used to record the year's net profit before it is transferred to the owner's capital
a general ledger account showing the total of a subsidiary ledger, such as all customers' balances
questions.explanation: The Accounts Receivable control account holds the total of the individual customer accounts kept in the subsidiary ledger; Accounts Payable and Inventories controls work the same way.

questions.stem: Why do businesses use control accounts for accounts receivable, accounts payable and inventories?
options: they let the business avoid recording GST on its credit transactions
they guarantee that customers will pay their accounts on time
they keep the general ledger short and allow the subsidiary ledger to be checked against one total
they remove the need to keep any separate records of individual customers and suppliers at all
questions.explanation: Detailed records go in the subsidiary ledgers, while the general ledger holds one total. Comparing the two totals helps detect errors, and different staff can maintain each record.

questions.stem: The Accounts Receivable control account shows $18,400, but the customer accounts in the subsidiary ledger total $18,950. What should the business conclude?
options: an error has been made in one of the records and must be found before reporting
the subsidiary ledger is always right, so the control account should be increased
the difference is a bad debt and should be written off as an expense
the difference is GST and should be paid to the ATO
questions.explanation: The control account and subsidiary ledger should agree, so a difference signals an error, such as a transaction posted to one record but not the other. Simply adjusting one figure or writing off the difference could hide the mistake.

questions.stem: When a credit sale of inventory is entered through the sales function of a computerised accounting package, what happens?
options: the package records the sale in cash at bank, because all sales are treated as cash sales by the software
the package automatically updates Accounts Receivable, Sales, GST, Inventories and Cost of Goods Sold
the user must post each part of the sale to the general ledger by hand afterwards
only the customer's account is updated, and the ledger is updated at year end
questions.explanation: A computerised package posts each transaction to every affected account immediately, including inventory and cost of goods sold under the perpetual system. This reduces errors but depends on accurate entry.

questions.stem: An aged accounts receivable report from a computerised package shows each customer's balance split into current, 30, 60 and 90+ days. What is its main use?
options: to list the amounts the business owes to its suppliers
to identify overdue accounts so they can be followed up
to calculate the depreciation on the business's equipment
to show the business's net profit for each customer
questions.explanation: The ageing shows how long amounts have been owing, so the business can chase overdue accounts and review credit for slow payers. Amounts owed to suppliers appear in an accounts payable report.

questions.stem: An aged accounts receivable report shows that one customer owes $3,000, all in the 90+ days column, and has placed a new order on credit. What is the best response?
options: add the new order to the 90+ days column so all the amounts are together
contact the customer about the overdue amount and hold further credit until it is paid
fill the new order on credit, as a large customer always pays eventually
remove the customer's balance from the report so that the totals look better to the owner
questions.explanation: An account over 90 days old is a collection risk, so the business should follow up and stop extending credit until it is settled. Hiding or misclassifying the balance would make the report unreliable.

questions.stem: How does a computerised accounting package determine the cost of goods sold and the value of inventories on hand?
options: it asks the user to estimate both figures at the end of each month
it updates both automatically from the cost of each item purchased and sold
it waits for an annual stocktake before calculating either figure
it uses the selling price of the goods as their cost
questions.explanation: Inventory items are set up with their costs, so every purchase and sale updates quantities, cost of goods sold and inventory value in real time. Stocktakes are still needed to find discrepancies such as theft.
